claims.text: A W–Mo–Ta–Nb–V refractory high-entropy alloy can be fabricated by a powder-based route with a single or predominantly BCC microstructure.
Refractory high-entropy alloys can retain a BCC phase at elevated temperatures.
The proposed W–Mo–Ta–Nb–V alloy will have a stable BCC phase near 660 °C.
Exposure to molten aluminum will produce a slow-growing, adherent passivating oxide or other refractory surface scale.
The constituent refractory elements have intrinsically high melting temperatures.
The constituent refractory elements have low chemical reactivity toward molten aluminum.
High melting temperatures and low chemical reactivity will limit dissolution of the alloy in molten aluminum.
High melting temperatures and low chemical reactivity will limit interdiffusion between the alloy and molten aluminum.
A protective refractory surface scale will hinder aluminum wetting.
A protective refractory surface scale will hinder erosion and preserve the underlying alloy structure.
The refractory high-entropy alloy will resist erosion by high-temperature liquid aluminum better than conventional hot-dip-plating materials.
The refractory high-entropy alloy will exhibit significantly lower weight loss than a conventional substrate under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
The refractory high-entropy alloy will exhibit less surface degradation than a conventional substrate.
The refractory high-entropy alloy will provide improved component durability under hot-dip aluminum plating conditions.
Carbon steels and other conventional hot-dip equipment materials corrode rapidly in high-temperature molten aluminum.
The proposed protection is expected to remain effective near 660 °C over typical service durations.
Performance under temperatures substantially above 660 °C or under severe mechanical stress is uncertain.
Long-term chemical compatibility with liquid aluminum and the robustness of a passivating scale during industrial cycling have not been fully quantified.
